@@@ USER
Build a simple to-do list in plain HTML and JavaScript that remembers the tasks after a page reload. Add, toggle done and delete.
@@@ ASSISTANT
Keep the tasks in an array, save it to `localStorage` as JSON after every change, and redraw the list from the array. One click listener on the `<ul>` handles every button (event delegation), so new items need no extra listeners.

`index.html`:

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>To-do list</title>
  <style>
    body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; max-width: 420px; margin: 40px auto; padding: 0 16px; }
    li { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; gap: 8px; padding: 8px 0; border-bottom: 1px solid #ddd; cursor: pointer; }
    li.done span { text-decoration: line-through; color: #888; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>To-do</h1>
  <form id="form">
    <input id="text" placeholder="New task" required>
    <button>Add</button>
  </form>
  <ul id="list"></ul>
  <script src="app.js"></script>
</body>
</html>
```

`app.js`:

```js
const form = document.querySelector("#form");
const input = document.querySelector("#text");
const list = document.querySelector("#list");
const KEY = "todos";

function load() {
  try {
    return JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY)) || [];
  } catch {
    return []; // corrupted or blocked storage: start empty instead of crashing
  }
}

let todos = load();

function save() {
  localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(todos));
}

function render() {
  list.innerHTML = "";
  for (const todo of todos) {
    const li = document.createElement("li");
    li.dataset.id = todo.id;
    li.className = todo.done ? "done" : "";

    const label = document.createElement("span");
    label.textContent = todo.text; // textContent, never innerHTML, for user text

    const del = document.createElement("button");
    del.textContent = "Delete";
    del.dataset.action = "delete";

    li.append(label, del);
    list.appendChild(li);
  }
}

form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
  event.preventDefault(); // stop the page from reloading
  const text = input.value.trim();
  if (!text) return;
  todos.push({ id: Date.now(), text, done: false });
  save();
  render();
  form.reset();
  input.focus();
});

list.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const li = event.target.closest("li");
  if (!li) return;
  const id = Number(li.dataset.id);
  if (event.target.dataset.action === "delete") {
    todos = todos.filter((t) => t.id !== id);
  } else {
    const todo = todos.find((t) => t.id === id);
    todo.done = !todo.done;
  }
  save();
  render();
});

render();
```

Why it is built this way:
- The array is the single source of truth. The page is always redrawn from it, so the screen and the saved data cannot disagree.
- `closest("li")` finds the list item even if the click landed on the text inside it.
- `localStorage` stores only strings, so use `JSON.stringify` to save and `JSON.parse` to load, and wrap loading in `try/catch`.
- `localStorage` belongs to one browser on one device. For data shared across devices you need a server.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
How do I add a dark mode toggle that follows the system setting and remembers my choice?
@@@ ASSISTANT
Define colors as CSS variables, override them for dark, and flip a `data-theme` attribute on `<html>`. Use the system preference as the default and `localStorage` for the user's choice.

CSS:

```css
:root {
  --bg: #ffffff;
  --text: #1d2330;
  --card: #f3f4f7;
}

/* Follow the system when the user has not chosen */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root:not([data-theme="light"]) {
    --bg: #12151c;
    --text: #e8eaf0;
    --card: #1d222d;
  }
}

/* Explicit choice wins over the system setting */
:root[data-theme="dark"] {
  --bg: #12151c;
  --text: #e8eaf0;
  --card: #1d222d;
}

body {
  background: var(--bg);
  color: var(--text);
  transition: background 0.2s, color 0.2s;
}

.card {
  background: var(--card);
  padding: 16px;
  border-radius: 12px;
}
```

JavaScript:

```js
const root = document.documentElement;
const button = document.querySelector("#theme-toggle");

function systemTheme() {
  return window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches ? "dark" : "light";
}

function currentTheme() {
  return root.dataset.theme || systemTheme();
}

function applyTheme(theme) {
  root.dataset.theme = theme;
  button.textContent = theme === "dark" ? "Light mode" : "Dark mode";
  button.setAttribute("aria-pressed", String(theme === "dark"));
}

try {
  const saved = localStorage.getItem("theme");
  if (saved === "dark" || saved === "light") root.dataset.theme = saved;
} catch {}

applyTheme(currentTheme());

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  const next = currentTheme() === "dark" ? "light" : "dark";
  applyTheme(next);
  try {
    localStorage.setItem("theme", next);
  } catch {}
});
```

Tips:
- To avoid a white flash on load, put the small "read saved theme and set `data-theme`" part in an inline `<script>` in the `<head>`, before the page is drawn.
- Add `<meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">` so form controls and scrollbars match the theme.
- Check contrast in both themes; light gray text on a dark background is a common accessibility mistake.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
Give me the Flexbox patterns I will use most: center something, a navbar with the logo on the left and links on the right, and a footer that stays at the bottom.
@@@ ASSISTANT
Flexbox lays out items along one direction (the main axis). `justify-content` aligns along that axis, `align-items` across it.

**1. Center anything, both ways:**

```css
.center {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: center; /* horizontal */
  align-items: center;     /* vertical */
  min-height: 100vh;
}
```

**2. Navbar: logo on the left, links on the right:**

```css
.navbar {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between;
  align-items: center;
  padding: 12px 24px;
}
.navbar ul {
  display: flex;
  gap: 16px;
  list-style: none;
  margin: 0;
  padding: 0;
}
```

```html
<nav class="navbar">
  <a href="/" class="logo">MyApp</a>
  <ul>
    <li><a href="/docs">Docs</a></li>
    <li><a href="/pricing">Pricing</a></li>
    <li><a href="/login">Log in</a></li>
  </ul>
</nav>
```

**3. Sticky footer (footer at the bottom even on short pages):**

```css
body {
  min-height: 100vh;
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  margin: 0;
}
main {
  flex: 1; /* takes all the leftover height, pushing the footer down */
}
```

**4. Cards that wrap onto new lines:**

```css
.row {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: 16px;
}
.row > .card {
  flex: 1 1 240px; /* grow, shrink, start at 240px */
}
```

Quick guide:
- `gap` spaces items without margin hacks.
- `flex: 1` means "share the free space equally".
- Use Flexbox for one row or column of items, and CSS Grid when you need rows and columns together.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
How do I validate a signup form in JavaScript and send it to a server as JSON?
@@@ ASSISTANT
Let the browser do basic checks with HTML attributes (`required`, `type="email"`, `minlength`), then add your own rules in JavaScript, and send the data with `fetch` only when everything is valid.

```html
<form id="signup" novalidate>
  <label>Email <input name="email" type="email" required></label>
  <p class="error" data-for="email"></p>

  <label>Password <input name="password" type="password" minlength="8" required></label>
  <p class="error" data-for="password"></p>

  <button type="submit">Create account</button>
  <p id="result" role="status"></p>
</form>
```

```js
const form = document.querySelector("#signup");
const result = document.querySelector("#result");

function showError(name, message) {
  document.querySelector(`.error[data-for="${name}"]`).textContent = message;
}

function validate(data) {
  const errors = {};
  if (!/^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/.test(data.email)) {
    errors.email = "Enter a valid email address.";
  }
  if (data.password.length < 8) {
    errors.password = "Use at least 8 characters.";
  } else if (!/\d/.test(data.password)) {
    errors.password = "Include at least one number.";
  }
  return errors;
}

form.addEventListener("submit", async (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const data = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form));

  showError("email", "");
  showError("password", "");
  const errors = validate(data);
  if (Object.keys(errors).length > 0) {
    for (const [name, message] of Object.entries(errors)) showError(name, message);
    return;
  }

  try {
    const response = await fetch("/api/signup", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify(data),
    });
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Server error ${response.status}`);
    result.textContent = "Account created!";
    form.reset();
  } catch (error) {
    result.textContent = `Could not sign up: ${error.message}`;
  }
});
```

Important points:
- `novalidate` turns off the browser's own pop-ups so your messages are used; remove it if you prefer the built-in ones.
- `new FormData(form)` reads every named field; `Object.fromEntries` turns it into a plain object.
- **Client-side validation is for convenience only.** Anyone can skip it, so the server must validate again.
- Never log or display passwords, and send them only over HTTPS.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
What is the difference between Promise.all, allSettled, race and any in JavaScript? Show a timeout helper too.
@@@ ASSISTANT
- `Promise.all`: waits for all; if any one fails, the whole thing fails right away.
- `Promise.allSettled`: waits for all and reports each result, whether it succeeded or failed; it never rejects.
- `Promise.race`: finishes with whichever promise settles first (success or failure).
- `Promise.any`: finishes with the first one that succeeds; fails only if all fail.

```js
const wait = (ms, value, fail = false) =>
  new Promise((resolve, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => (fail ? reject(new Error(value)) : resolve(value)), ms)
  );

function withTimeout(promise, ms) {
  const timeout = new Promise((_, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => reject(new Error(`timed out after ${ms} ms`)), ms)
  );
  return Promise.race([promise, timeout]);
}

async function main() {
  console.log(await Promise.all([wait(30, "a"), wait(10, "b"), wait(20, "c")]));

  try {
    await Promise.all([wait(10, "ok"), wait(20, "boom", true)]);
  } catch (error) {
    console.log("all failed:", error.message);
  }

  const settled = await Promise.allSettled([wait(10, "ok"), wait(20, "boom", true)]);
  console.log(settled.map((r) => r.status));

  console.log(await Promise.race([wait(50, "slow"), wait(10, "fast")]));
  console.log(await Promise.any([wait(10, "bad", true), wait(30, "good")]));

  try {
    await withTimeout(wait(200, "too late"), 50);
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(error.message);
  }
}

main();
```

Output:

```
[ 'a', 'b', 'c' ]
all failed: boom
[ 'fulfilled', 'rejected' ]
fast
good
timed out after 50 ms
```

When to use which:
- Loading several independent pieces for one screen where all are required: `all`.
- A dashboard where one broken widget must not break the others: `allSettled`.
- A timeout, or "use the fastest server": `race`.
- Results come in the same order as the input, not the order they finish.
- Run independent requests together (`await Promise.all([...])`) instead of one after another with separate `await` lines; it can be several times faster.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
Show the JavaScript array methods I need every day (map, filter, find, reduce, sort, some, every, includes) with a list of objects.
@@@ ASSISTANT
These methods return new values and do not change the original array (except `sort`, which sorts in place).

```js
const products = [
  { name: "Keyboard", price: 45, category: "tech", stock: 12 },
  { name: "Mouse", price: 20, category: "tech", stock: 0 },
  { name: "Notebook", price: 5, category: "office", stock: 100 },
  { name: "Monitor", price: 180, category: "tech", stock: 4 },
  { name: "Pen", price: 2, category: "office", stock: 250 },
];

// map: one output per item
console.log(products.map((p) => p.name));

// filter: keep the items that pass the test
const available = products.filter((p) => p.stock > 0);
console.log(available.length);

// find: the first match (or undefined)
console.log(products.find((p) => p.price > 100)?.name);

// reduce: combine into one value
const inventoryValue = products.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p.price * p.stock, 0);
console.log(inventoryValue);

// sort: copy first so the original order is kept
const cheapestFirst = [...products].sort((a, b) => a.price - b.price);
console.log(cheapestFirst.map((p) => p.name));

// some / every / includes
console.log(products.some((p) => p.stock === 0));
console.log(products.every((p) => p.price > 1));
console.log(["tech", "office"].includes(products[0].category));

// group by category with reduce
const byCategory = products.reduce((groups, p) => {
  (groups[p.category] ||= []).push(p.name);
  return groups;
}, {});
console.log(byCategory);

// chain them
const report = products
  .filter((p) => p.category === "tech" && p.stock > 0)
  .map((p) => `${p.name}: $${p.price}`)
  .join(", ");
console.log(report);
```

Output:

```
[ 'Keyboard', 'Mouse', 'Notebook', 'Monitor', 'Pen' ]
4
Monitor
2260
[ 'Pen', 'Notebook', 'Mouse', 'Keyboard', 'Monitor' ]
true
true
true
{
  tech: [ 'Keyboard', 'Mouse', 'Monitor' ],
  office: [ 'Notebook', 'Pen' ]
}
Keyboard: $45, Monitor: $180
```

Mistakes to avoid:
- `a.sort()` without a compare function sorts numbers as text (`[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]`). Always pass `(a, b) => a - b`.
- Forgetting the initial value in `reduce` (`0` or `{}`) breaks on empty arrays.
- `forEach` cannot be stopped with `break`; use a `for...of` loop or `some`/`find` when you need to stop early.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
My JavaScript throws "Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'addEventListener')". Why?

```html
<head>
  <script src="app.js"></script>
</head>
<body>
  <button id="save">Save</button>
</body>
```

```js
document.querySelector("#save").addEventListener("click", () => {
  console.log("saved");
});
```
@@@ ASSISTANT
**Cause:** the script is in `<head>`, so it runs before the browser has created the button. `document.querySelector("#save")` finds nothing and returns `null`, and `null` has no `addEventListener`.

**Fix 1 (best): add `defer`.** The script is downloaded early but runs only after the whole HTML has been parsed.

```html
<head>
  <script src="app.js" defer></script>
</head>
<body>
  <button id="save">Save</button>
</body>
```

**Fix 2:** move the `<script>` tag to the end of `<body>`, just before `</body>`.

**Fix 3:** wait for the page inside the JavaScript:

```js
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => {
  document.querySelector("#save").addEventListener("click", () => {
    console.log("saved");
  });
});
```

Changes made:
- Fix 1 only adds the word `defer` to the script tag; `app.js` stays the same.

If the error remains after that, check for a spelling difference: `id="save"` in the HTML must match `#save` in the JavaScript exactly, including capital letters. Also make sure the element is not created later by other code.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
Why is `this` undefined inside my method when I pass it as a callback in JavaScript? How do I fix it?
@@@ ASSISTANT
In JavaScript, `this` depends on how a function is *called*, not where it is written. `obj.method()` sets `this` to `obj`. But when you hand the method over as a bare function (`setTimeout(obj.method)`, an event handler), it is called with no object, so `this` is lost.

```js
class Counter {
  constructor() {
    this.count = 0;
  }

  incrementBroken() {
    this.count += 1;
  }

  // Fix 1: an arrow function property keeps `this` from where it was created
  incrementArrow = () => {
    this.count += 1;
  };
}

const c = new Counter();

const lost = c.incrementBroken;
try {
  lost();
} catch (error) {
  console.log("broken:", error.message);
}

// Fix 2: bind
const bound = c.incrementBroken.bind(c);
bound();
console.log("bound:", c.count);

// Fix 1 in use
const arrow = c.incrementArrow;
arrow();
arrow();
console.log("arrow:", c.count);

// Fix 3: wrap it in an arrow function at the call site
const wrapped = () => c.incrementBroken();
wrapped();
console.log("wrapped:", c.count);
```

Output:

```
broken: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'count')
bound: 1
arrow: 3
wrapped: 4
```

Which fix to use:
- Class methods used as event handlers (`button.addEventListener("click", this.handleClick)`): define them as arrow-function properties, or bind them once in the constructor.
- A one-off callback: wrap it, `() => obj.method()`.
- Arrow functions do not have their own `this`; they use the surrounding one. That is why they work here, and why you should not use them as object methods that need `this` to be the object.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
I get a CORS error in the browser console: "blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header". What is it and how do I fix it?
@@@ ASSISTANT
**What it is:** browsers only let a web page read a response from another origin (different domain, port or protocol) if that server says it is allowed. Your page on `http://localhost:5173` calling an API on `http://localhost:3000` is a different origin. The request may reach the server, but the browser hides the response from your JavaScript because the server did not send an `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header.

**The fix is on the server**, not in your front-end code. A minimal Node server using only the built-in `http` module:

```js
const http = require("http");

const ALLOWED_ORIGIN = "http://localhost:5173";

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  res.setHeader("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", ALLOWED_ORIGIN);
  res.setHeader("Access-Control-Allow-Methods", "GET, POST, OPTIONS");
  res.setHeader("Access-Control-Allow-Headers", "Content-Type");

  // Preflight: the browser asks permission first for POST with JSON, custom headers, etc.
  if (req.method === "OPTIONS") {
    res.writeHead(204);
    res.end();
    return;
  }

  if (req.method === "GET" && req.url === "/api/hello") {
    res.writeHead(200, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
    res.end(JSON.stringify({ message: "hello" }));
    return;
  }

  res.writeHead(404, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
  res.end(JSON.stringify({ error: "not found" }));
});

server.listen(3000, () => console.log("API on http://localhost:3000"));
```

With Express, the `cors` package does the same: `app.use(cors({ origin: "http://localhost:5173" }))`.

Things to know:
- Allow your real front-end origin, not `*`, if requests carry cookies or login tokens. `*` is fine only for public data.
- If the preflight (`OPTIONS`) request fails, you will see the same error even though the real request would work. Check the Network tab for it.
- During development, a proxy avoids CORS completely: Vite's `server.proxy` forwards `/api` to the backend, so the browser only talks to one origin.
- CORS does not protect your server. It only controls what browsers let pages read. Authentication must still be checked on the server.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
Give me a good mobile-first CSS starting point: fluid text sizes, comfortable line length, and a layout that changes at a tablet breakpoint.
@@@ ASSISTANT
Write the phone layout first (single column, no media queries), then use `min-width` media queries to add features on bigger screens. Use `clamp()` so text scales smoothly between a minimum and maximum.

```css
:root {
  --space: 16px;
  --radius: 12px;
  --max-width: 1100px;
}

*,
*::before,
*::after {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

body {
  margin: 0;
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  font-size: clamp(1rem, 0.95rem + 0.25vw, 1.125rem);
  line-height: 1.6;
}

h1 {
  font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 1.2rem + 2.5vw, 3rem);
  line-height: 1.15;
}

img,
video {
  max-width: 100%;
  height: auto;
}

.container {
  width: min(100% - 2 * var(--space), var(--max-width));
  margin-inline: auto;
}

/* Comfortable reading width: about 60-75 characters */
.prose {
  max-width: 65ch;
}

/* Phone: one column */
.layout {
  display: grid;
  gap: var(--space);
}

/* Tablet and up: sidebar + content */
@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .layout {
    grid-template-columns: 240px 1fr;
  }
}

/* Large screens: more breathing room */
@media (min-width: 1200px) {
  .layout {
    gap: calc(var(--space) * 2);
  }
}

/* Respect users who ask for less motion */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  * {
    animation: none !important;
    transition: none !important;
  }
}
```

Why these choices:
- `clamp(min, preferred, max)` keeps text readable on a small phone and not oversized on a big monitor, with no breakpoints.
- `max-width: 100%` on images stops them overflowing the screen, and `height: auto` keeps their proportions.
- `65ch` is about 65 characters wide, the range where long text is easiest to read.
- Test with the browser's device toolbar (F12, then the phone icon) and also by dragging the window narrow; the layout should never scroll sideways.
@@@ END
